Independent reading lets them extend that knowledge of myths, heroes and retellings with a book of their own.","enduringUnderstanding":"Stories carry the fears and values of the people who tell them, and readers grow by choosing texts and reading them with purpose.","futureLessons":"Students will bring their independent reading and reading plan into Investigation 2, starting with Chapter 13 in Lesson 20, and use it for homework logs and cross-text comparison.","performanceTask":"The Performance Task, Shared Stories, Shared Lessons, asks for multi-source evidence. A well-chosen independent book gives students another source to compare and cite."},"vocabulary":[{"word":"preview","definition":"to look at the cover, summary and first page of a book before reading to decide what it is about","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"plan","definition":"a clear set of steps for when, where and how much you will read","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"retelling","definition":"a new version of an older story, with changes that fit a new time or audience","tier":"support"},{"word":"value","definition":"something a person or culture believes is important","tier":"support"}],"texts":[{"title":"Independent Reading List","pages":"Student choice"},{"title":"The Lightning Thief","author":"Rick Riordan","pages":"Chapters 1-12 (for connections only)"}]},"sections":[{"kind":"launch","title":"Launch","purpose":"Students recall what kinds of stories and heroes they have enjoyed in the unit and start thinking about what they want to read next.","activities":[{"id":"launch-turn-and-talk","title":"What Makes You Keep Reading?","minutes":5,"standards":[],"routine":"Turn and Talk","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Turn to a partner. Name one moment in The Lightning Thief so far that made you want to keep reading. Then name one kind of book you would like to read next."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Today is a Flex Day. You will choose a book from our Independent Reading List, talk about it in a small group, and make a plan to read it."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What made you want to turn the page in Chapters 1-12? Think of Percy's first monster attack or the arrival at Camp Half-Blood."},{"type":"sample-response","text":"I wanted to keep reading after Mrs. Dodds turned into a Fury at the museum, because I needed to know if Percy was imagining it or if everyone was lying to him. I like books where something strange happens right away."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Keep this to five minutes. While students talk, glance at the Independent Reading List and decide which students you will pull for each Huddle. Pull students who have not yet chosen a book first."}]}]},{"kind":"learning-in-action","title":"Learning in Action","purpose":"Students rotate through three short Huddles: choosing a book, a Content Knowledge Huddle about the chosen book, and making a reading plan.","activities":[{"id":"huddle-1-choose-book","title":"Huddle 1: Choosing a Book From the List","minutes":14,"standards":[],"routine":"Huddle","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"Independent Reading List","pages":"Whole list"},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"Pull students who have not chosen a book, who keep switching books, or who choose only by cover. All other students begin independent choice work: previewing two books from the list and jotting one reason each might be a good fit. Students not in the Huddle should keep the list in front of them."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"If your class is working on other skills, this Huddle can also serve students who need help with other unit reteaching. Use any Arc lesson (such as evidence from L4-L18) as the reteach if your data shows that need."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"**Reteach.** Readers *preview* a book before choosing it: they read the cover, the summary and the first page. They ask whether the book connects to ideas from our unit, such as heroes, myths, fears and values, or retellings. They also ask whether they can read it with understanding and interest."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"When Percy reads about Greek myths, he already knows a little about them. We choose books the same way, by looking for a spark of interest and something to connect to."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"**Guided Practice.** Have each student pick up one book from the list and preview it for two minutes."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What does the cover or summary tell you about this book? What do you notice about the main character or the problem?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The summary says the main character finds out she has a secret power, like Percy finding out he is a demigod. I think this book will have some of the same feeling of a hidden identity."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Read the first page quietly. Is it easy to follow and interesting enough that you want to keep going?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Yes, the first page has action right away and the words are not too hard. I could read this at home without getting stuck."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"**Quick Check.** Students write one sentence: *I chose ___ because ___.* Circulate and check that each student has named a book and a real reason."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support English learners in previewing a book and explaining a choice in complete sentences.","sayAsk":"Say: Point to the title, then tell your partner what the book is about. Ask: Why do you want to read this book? Frames: I chose ___ because ___. The cover shows ___. The summary says ___. This book is like The Lightning Thief because ___. Model: You said 'it looks good' - we can say: 'The summary says the main character faces a danger, and I like adventure stories.'","watchFor":"If a student only says 'it looks good,' then prompt: 'What on the cover or in the summary made you think so?' If a student cannot read the first page, then offer a book at a lower level or a partner read-aloud. Success: the student names a book and gives one reason using the frame."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: choosing from too many books","tryThis":"Narrow the list to three books and ask the student to preview each for one minute before choosing."},{"situation":"Struggling with: choosing a book that is too hard","tryThis":"Have the student read aloud one paragraph. If more than five words are unfamiliar, suggest another book on the list."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask the student to explain how the book might connect to myths, heroes or retellings from the unit, and to predict one theme."}]}]},{"id":"huddle-2-content-knowledge","title":"Huddle 2: Content Knowledge Huddle About My Book","minutes":14,"standards":[],"routine":"Huddle","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"Independent Reading List","pages":"Student's chosen book"},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"Pull students who have chosen a book. Others work independently: reread the first page of their chosen book and write two questions they hope the book will answer."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"**Reteach.** Content knowledge is what we already know and what we need to learn about a topic. Good readers activate what they know before reading, as we did with myths in Lesson 4, and ask questions that help them build more knowledge. Remind students how they compared Percy with Soongoora, Raven, the Hero Twins and Perseus. The same moves of looking for fears, values and patterns work for any book."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Before we read, let's talk about what we already know and what we want to find out about your book."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"**Guided Practice.** Each student shares briefly about the chosen book while the group listens."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What do you already know about the topic, setting or kind of story in your book?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"My book is about a girl at a camp for kids with special talents. I already know about camps like that from The Lightning Thief, where kids train and learn who they are."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What do you predict the main character might fear or value? What clue in the cover, title or summary makes you think so?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"I think she values her friends because the summary says she will risk everything to save them. Percy values his mom, so I will watch for how they are alike and different."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What is one question you hope the book will answer?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"I want to know why she has to hide her power and who she can trust."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"**Quick Check.** Students write a three-part note: *What I know, what I predict, what I wonder.* Listen for a connection to a unit idea such as heroes, fears or values."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help English learners use background knowledge and predictions to talk about a book with academic language.","sayAsk":"Say: Tell your partner one thing you already know. Ask: What do you predict? What do you wonder? Frames: I already know ___. I predict ___ because the text says ___. I wonder ___. This book is similar to The Lightning Thief because ___. Model: You said 'she is like Percy' - we can say: 'The main character is like Percy because she also discovers a hidden identity.'","watchFor":"If a student predicts without a reason, then prompt: 'What clue did you see?' If a student offers only one word, then give the frame and let the student say it to a partner first. Success: the student gives a prediction with a clue and one question."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: not knowing anything about the book's topic","tryThis":"Use the cover and summary together and ask, 'What do you notice? What does this remind you of from our unit?'"},{"situation":"Struggling with: only retelling the summary","tryThis":"Offer the frame 'I wonder why ___' and model one question about a character's choice."},{"situation":"Ready for extension","tryThis":"Ask the student to compare the book's likely hero with Percy, using one value and one fear, and to say how the book might retell an older story."}]}]},{"id":"huddle-3-reading-plan","title":"Huddle 3: Making My Reading Plan","minutes":12,"standards":[],"routine":"Huddle","blocks":[{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"Pull students who have chosen and previewed a book and need a plan. Others work independently, reading the first chapter or ten pages of their book and marking one spot that raises a question."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"**Reteach.** A reading *plan* names when, where and how much you will read, and what you will do to remember what you read. Strong readers set realistic goals, such as pages per night, and track them in a log. Refer to the homework routine students already use."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Heroes in myths do not succeed by luck. They prepare. Percy trained at camp before the quest. Let's prepare for your reading the same way."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"**Guided Practice.** Students complete a plan with: book title, total pages, finish date, pages per night, reading time and place, and one way to hold their thinking (sticky notes, log entries or questions)."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How many pages can you realistically read each night, and when will you read?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"My book has 240 pages, so I can read 15 pages a night for about 16 days. I will read right after dinner at the kitchen table."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What could get in the way of your plan, and what will you do about it?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Sports practice on Tuesdays and Thursdays might make me tired. On those days I will read ten pages on the bus instead of fifteen."},{"type":"paragraph","audience":"teacher","text":"**Quick Check.** Each student states the plan aloud to a partner in one sentence: *I will read ___ pages each ___ at ___ so I can finish by ___.* Check that the numbers add up."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support English learners in stating a plan with future-tense language and numbers.","sayAsk":"Say: Tell your partner your plan. Ask: How many pages each night? Where will you read? Frames: I will read ___ pages each night. I will read at ___. I will finish by ___. If something gets in the way, I will ___. Model: You said 'read a lot' - we can say: 'I will read fifteen pages every night.'","watchFor":"If a student gives a vague amount, then prompt: 'Give me a number.' If a plan is not realistic, then ask: 'Is that possible on a busy night?' Success: the student states a specific pages-per-night goal and a time and place."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: setting a realistic goal","tryThis":"Start from the finish date and divide the pages together on a calculator or sticky note."},{"type":"situation-placeholder-removed","tryThis":""}]}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Students reflect on their book choice and plan.","activities":[{"id":"look-back-quick-write","title":"My Book and My Plan","minutes":5,"standards":[],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Write 3-4 sentences: Which book did you choose? Why? What is your reading plan? What question do you hope your book answers?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"I chose a book about a girl who discovers a secret power because it reminds me of Percy finding out he is a demigod. I plan to read fifteen pages every night after dinner. I hope the book answers why she has to hide her power."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Invite two or three students to share. Collect the plans or check them against the homework reading log in the next few days."}]}]}]},"digest":{"summary":"Students chose a book from the Independent Reading List, discussed what they know and predict about it in a Content Knowledge Huddle, and wrote a realistic reading plan. This Flex Day carries no focus standards and prepares students to read independently as they move into Investigation 2.","keyActivities":["Huddle 1: Choosing a Book From the List","Huddle 2: Content Knowledge Huddle About My Book","Huddle 3: Making My Reading Plan","Look Back Quick Write on book and plan"],"vocabularyTaught":["preview","plan","retelling","value"],"standardsCovered":[]}}
